en.note:
The idea

English has a few diminutive endings, like -ie, -y or -let (doggie, booklet), but mostly just says "little". Dutch has one family of endings, all based on -je: huis → huisje (little house), kat → katje (kitten). The Dutch and the Flemish use diminutives far more than English speakers do: not only for small things, but also to show affection, to make a sentence sound lighter and more casual, or with a completely new meaning.

Two fixed rules

  • A diminutive is always het, even if the base noun is a de-word: de hond → het hondje.
  • The plural is always -s: het hondje → de hondjes.

Which ending?

The form depends on the final sound of the word. You don't have to memorize it: it's the one that's easiest to pronounce.

endingwhenexamples
-jeafter most consonants (p, t, k, d, f, s...)boek → boekje, hond → hondje, huis → huisje
-tjeafter a vowel; after l, n, r with a long vowel before them; after final -el, -en, -erauto → autootje, stoel → stoeltje, deur → deurtje, tafel → tafeltje
-pjeafter m with a long vowel before it, and after -lm, -rmboom → boompje, film → filmpje
-etjeafter a short stressed vowel + l, m, n, r, ng (the consonant doubles)bal → balletje, man → mannetje, ring → ringetje
-kjeafter unstressed -ing: ng becomes nkkoning → koninkje

In words ending in a, o, u the vowel is doubled so that it stays long: auto → autootje, menu → menuutje.

Diminutives with their own meaning

Some diminutives have become words in their own right, to be learned as such:

  • het broodje: a sandwich, a bread roll (not "a little bread"). Een broodje kaas = a cheese sandwich.
  • het koekje: a cookie.
  • het kopje: a cup (of coffee or tea). Een kopje koffie.
  • het ijsje: an ice cream (one serving, a cone).
  • het biertje: a beer, said in a casual, friendly way.
  • het meisje: girl (unit 3).
  • een beetje: a bit, a little. Ik spreek een beetje Nederlands.

Watch out: typical mistakes for English speakers

  • Keeping the article of the base word: de hondje → het hondje.
  • Making the plural with -en: twee huisjen → twee huisjes.
  • Always just adding -je: autoje, balje → autootje, balletje.
  • Translating "a sandwich" word for word or as een klein brood → een broodje.
  • Avoiding diminutives because English rarely uses them: in Dutch een kopje koffie or een biertje sounds more natural than the plain word.
en.vlaams: In spoken Flemish the diminutive often ends in -ke instead of -je: "een manneke" (a little man), which gives us the name of Brussels' Manneken Pis. In a Belgian bar people happily order "een pintje", a glass of draft lager.
